title: Strang's two freedoms: the essential freedom of spontaneous rational motion survives absolute decrees; indifference does not
source_text: XIV. Ut autem decreta divina cum voluntatis humanae libertate conciliet, duplicem voluntatis libertatem distinguit. Unam latius & communius sumptam, quae voluntati essentialis est, & in eo consistit quod voluntas proprio suo motu, certoque rationis judicio movetur: Alteram sensu strictiore acceptam, quam constituit in quadam voluntatis indifferentia ad opposita duo vel plura. Decreta Dei quibus absolute voluntatis actus praedefiniti sunt, fatetur hanc posteriorem libertatem tollere, quandoquidem voluntatem ad unum praedeterminant, nec sinunt amplius eam indifferentem ut agat vel non agat: sed ex ejus sententia voluntatem non privant libertate priori, quia haec optime consistunt, ut voluntas rationis judicium sequatur, & motu naturae suae consentaneo feratur, & tamen ad agendum a Deo praedefinita, & in tempore praedeterminata sit; quoniam scilicet, Deus voluntatem movet suaviter, & eo modo qui congruit & conveniens est naturae voluntatis.
pass_a_gloss: XIV. But that he may reconcile the divine decrees with the freedom of the human will, he distinguishes a double freedom of the will. One taken more widely and commonly, which is essential to the will, and consists in this that the will is moved by its own proper motion, and a certain judgement of reason: The other taken in a stricter sense, which he places in a certain indifference of the will to two or more opposites. The decrees of God by which acts of the will are absolutely predefined, he confesses take away this latter freedom, since they predetermine the will to one, nor allow it any longer to be indifferent to act or not act: but in his opinion they do not deprive the will of the former freedom, because these stand together very well, that the will follow the judgement of reason, and be borne by a motion agreeable to its nature, and yet be predefined to act by God, and predetermined in time; since namely, God moves the will sweetly, and in that way which is congruous and suitable to the nature of the will.
pass_b_english: To reconcile the divine decrees with the freedom of the human will, he distinguishes two kinds of freedom of the will. One, taken more broadly and commonly, is essential to the will: it consists in the will's being moved by its own motion and by a definite judgement of reason. The other, taken in a stricter sense, he locates in a kind of indifference of the will toward two or more opposites.

He admits that the decrees of God by which acts of the will are absolutely predefined remove this second freedom, since they predetermine the will to one thing and no longer leave it indifferent to act or not act.

But on his view they do not deprive the will of the first freedom. It fits perfectly well that the will should follow the judgement of reason and be carried by a motion in keeping with its nature, and yet be predefined by God to act and predetermined in time. For God moves the will gently, in a way that suits and befits the will's nature.
